evidence.quote: Calendula prefers cooler temperatures (< 85°F) and often stops blooming in extreme heat.
‘Coronet’ and ‘Pacific Beauty’ exhibit increased heat tolerance.
Plants may languish in prolonged hot summer weather but typically recover when cooler weather returns.

evidence.source_name: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
evidence.quote: Marigolds do not do well in hot summer weather or times of drought, but can be cut back to rejuvenate in the fall.
Pot marigold is generally not a warm-season plant but may be cut back in the spring to encourage fall regrowth.
Sow the seeds ¼ to ½ inches deep; light will inhibit germination.
Plant seeds ¼ inch deep when soil temperatures reach 60°F.

evidence.source_name: Eberle et al., ASA/CSSA/SSSA 2013 meeting abstract (USDA-ARS / UMN)
evidence.quote: Above 30°C calendula germination was 0%.

evidence.source_name: Eberle et al., ASA/CSSA/SSSA 2013 meeting abstract (USDA-ARS / UMN)
evidence.quote: Based on these data calendula seed should only be sown in the field if environmental temperature conditions are predicted to be below 30°C during seed germination.

evidence.source_name: Eberle et al. 2014, Industrial Crops and Products 52:199-204 (peer-reviewed; abstract on Experts@Minnesota)
evidence.quote: Calendula is adapted to temperate climate, but field studies in western Minnesota indicated that stand establishment was susceptible to high soil temperatures immediately after planting in spring.

evidence.source_name: NC State Extension (Maisano, commercial cut-flower note)
evidence.quote: Seeds germinate best at 70°F in continuous darkness and should emerge in about ten days.

calendula.hold_basis: G+M: seed fails to germinate above 30°C/86°F and the peer-reviewed authors explicitly say to sow only when forecast conditions stay below 30°C (G/S); mature plants prefer < 85°F and often stop blooming in extreme heat (M).
calendula.threshold_note: USU: 'prefers cooler temperatures (< 85°F) and often stops blooming in extreme heat' -> 85, matching the current value and the contract's mature-plant definition. Independent G corroboration: Eberle et al. 0% germination above 30°C (86°F) and 'sow only if ... predicted to be below 30°C'. Tension: Eberle's 30°C is soil/environment temperature during germination, while the app compares the forecast air HIGH; the two numbers (85 vs 86) agree closely anyway. Note the USU sentence's '< 85°F' is lost in tools/.doc_cache (the cache's tag stripper ate the literal '<'), so the cached copy reads 'prefers cooler temperatures (' ; the bytes are in fetched/ from a fresh fetch.

reason_tip_candidate.draft_seasoned: Hold calendula sowings when highs are running above about 85°F: the seed does not germinate above about 86°F (30°C), and researchers advise sowing only when conditions are forecast to stay below that. Mature plants also prefer temperatures under 85°F and often stop blooming in extreme heat.
reason_tip_candidate.draft_beginner: Wait for cooler weather to sow calendula. Its seeds will not sprout when it is hotter than about 86°F, and the plants often stop flowering in strong heat.

gaps: No extension page gives a germination upper limit in °F; the 86°F (30°C) figure is from the Eberle et al. peer-reviewed work and its meeting abstract.

The full Industrial Crops and Products paper was not fetched; quotes come from the Experts@Minnesota abstract and the ASA meeting abstract (the Experts@Minnesota abstract renders decimals as '30. °C', so the cleaner confex abstract is used for the threshold quotes).
calendula.notes: Coherent as held. Existing tip cal_germ_coolsoil says 'Calendula germinates poorly in hot soil' citing usu_ext + ufifas_ext; neither of those pages states that. Eberle et al. does, so a repoint (or add) of that tip's source to Eberle is suggested. USU and Wisconsin both note heat-tolerant cultivars / recovery when cool, which is a reason the hold is a pause, not an end of season.

evidence.quote: If planting by seed, keep in mind that they only germinate at temperatures between 65˚ and 75˚Fahrenheit.
The seed germinates in 10 to 14 days at temperatures between 65 and 75°F.
Cover the seed to exclude light.

evidence.source_name: MSU Extension Bulletin E-2239 (1990, archived; 'do not use for current recommendations')
evidence.quote: Seeds can be hard to germinate at temperatures over 75 to 80 degrees F.

evidence.source_name: NC State Extension, commercial pansy production (hortscans PDF)
evidence.quote: High temperatures (90° F) for longer than the first day reduce the percentage of germination from 90 to 55 percent.
They fade and should be discarded with the start of hot summer weather.
The pansies can be transplanted into the garden once the summer heat has been broken and cooler weather arrives.
The ideal temperature range for growing pansies is from about 40° F at night to 60° F during the day.
They produce their best flowers in the spring when the weather is mild, then fade and are usually discarded when really hot weather arrives.
If pansies are planted too early in the year while it’s still hot, they can exhibit yellowing foliage or elongated stems, which makes them more susceptible to diseases and insect pests.
Pansies thrive in air temperatures below 65˚ Fahrenheit at night.

evidence.source_name: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
evidence.quote: Pansy will eventually succumb to summer heat and should then be removed from the garden.
Plants often need to be removed during the summer in very hot areas as they get ragged.

viola.hold_basis: G+E+M: seed germinates only between 65 and 75°F (UF, two pages) and is hard to germinate above 75 to 80°F (MSU); transplants set out while still hot yellow and stretch (UF); plants fade with hot summer weather (Clemson, USU, NCSU, UC IPM).
viola.threshold_note: 75 = the top of UF's 'only germinate at temperatures between 65˚ and 75˚Fahrenheit' (also EDIS FP609; MSU E-2239 'hard to germinate at temperatures over 75 to 80 degrees F'). TENSION FOR TREVOR: the contract defines heat_threshold_f as the MATURE-plant number, and 75 is a GERMINATION (medium/soil) number. No T1 source found gives a mature-plant heat number in °F; the mature sources give only a cool ideal (USU 40°F night / 60°F day; UF below 65°F at night) or no number ('hot summer weather'). So 75 is sourced only as a germination ceiling, compared against forecast air highs. Also scope: every source is about garden pansy (Viola x wittrockiana; Clemson also covers Johnny-jump-ups); none is specific to V. cornuta.

reason_tip_candidate.draft_seasoned: Hold viola sowings while highs run above about 75°F: pansy seed germinates only between 65 and 75°F, and is hard to germinate above 75 to 80°F. Cover the seed to exclude light. Plants set out while it is still hot can yellow and stretch, so wait until summer heat breaks.
reason_tip_candidate.draft_beginner: Wait for cooler weather to sow violas. The seeds only sprout between about 65 and 75°F, and young plants set out in the heat turn yellow and leggy. Cover the seeds so they stay dark.

gaps: No T1 source gives a mature-plant heat-decline temperature in °F for any Viola; the 'fade above roughly 75°F' wording in the description/weather_trigger is not stated by UF's page (it gives 65-75°F for GERMINATION and <65°F nights for growth).
No T1 source specific to Viola cornuta or V. tricolor germination temperatures.
viola.notes: RE-VERIFY of the existing tip vio_germ_cool_dark: its ONLY source, Clemson HGIC pansies-and-johnny-jump-ups, does NOT contain any germination temperature, does not mention light or darkness for germination, and does not say warm soil inhibits germination (checked both the dataset cache 41afb0f5... and a fresh fetch). Clemson supports only the timing half: 'Sow seed indoors in late summer, six to eight weeks before transplanting.' The 65-75°F range and the cover-to-exclude-light instruction are supported by UF/IFAS EDIS FP609 and UF Gardening Solutions pansies (the latter is already cited elsewhere in this crop as uf_ifas). The tip's claim that light 'inhibits' germination is stronger than any source: EDIS says 'Cover the seed to exclude light', MSU E-2239 lists 'Continuous darkness' as a germination condition, and the NCSU commercial pansy PDF reports trials where uncovered seed germinated as well or better than covered seed. Suggest: repoint the tip to EDIS FP609 + UF Gardening Solutions and soften 'warm soil and light both inhibit' to what the quotes say. MSU E-2239 is archived and self-labeled not for current recommendations; the NCSU and MSU PDFs are two-column, so fetched/ text has a script-split DECOLUMNED copy appended (same bytes) so the quotes can be grepped.

evidence.quote: As summer temperatures rise, alyssum grown from seed may stop producing flowers.
Many sterile hybrids are available that have improved heat resistance and will last through the summer.
Seeds can also be sown in September for fall into winter flowers.
Like many brassicas, growth and flowering slows in hot weather ; the plants will look ragged in the heat of summer but will revive with cooler temperatures and last well into the fall.

evidence.source_name: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
evidence.quote: The mat-forming plant produces spreading mounds of fragrant white flowers from spring to first frost where the summers are cool (blooms will decline in hot summers).

evidence.source_name: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
evidence.quote: May stop blooming in the heat of summer, but can be rejuvenated.

evidence.section: refers to the vegetatively propagated Easy Breezy hybrid series, not seed-grown alyssum
evidence.quote: It’s compact and so heat tolerant that it will continue well after spring.

evidence.source_name: MSU Extension horticulture sheet (unofficial mirror on butterflywebsite.com)
evidence.quote: The seed germinates in 8 to 15 days at temperatures between 65 to 75 degrees.

sweet-alyssum.hold_basis: M: seed-grown plants slow, look ragged and may stop flowering as summer temperatures rise (Clemson, Wisconsin, NCSU); no T1 germination ceiling found.
sweet-alyssum.threshold_note: No T1 source gives a temperature for the bloom stall; every T1 quote is qualitative ('summer temperatures rise', 'hot weather', 'hot summers'). With threshold null the app falls back to 85°F, which is NOT sourced for this crop. The only number found is a 65 to 75°F germination range on an unofficial mirror of an MSU sheet (T2), which describes a germination temperature, not an upper limit.

reason_tip_candidate.draft_seasoned: Hold sweet alyssum sowings through hot spells: as summer temperatures rise, seed-grown alyssum slows, looks ragged and may stop flowering, then revives as it cools. Sow again in late summer or September for fall bloom, or grow a sterile heat-resistant hybrid.
reason_tip_candidate.draft_beginner: Sweet alyssum grown from seed slows down and may stop flowering in summer heat. Wait for cooler weather to sow more, or plant a heat-tolerant type.

gaps: No T1 germination temperature or germination upper limit for Lobularia maritima found (searched Clemson, Wisconsin, NCSU, UF, MSU, Penn State 'Sowing annual seeds' which gives spacing only).
No T1 temperature for the summer bloom stall.
sweet-alyssum.notes: INCOHERENCE CONFIRMED: heat_effect 'heat_tolerant' contradicts every T1 page; only sterile/vegetative hybrids (Snow Princess, Easy Breezy, Princess Group) are called heat tolerant, which is variety-level. Suggest heat_effect -> a bloom/quality-loss value with pause_in_heat true; the threshold stays a gap (fallback 85 is unsourced) unless Trevor accepts a qualitative hold.

evidence.quote: Nasturtiums do best in the cooler part of the year and will tend to decline when the temperatures get too hot.

evidence.source_name: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox (Tropaeolum genus page)
evidence.quote: Areas where the summer temperatures are somewhat cooler will allow this plant to perform at its best.

evidence.source_name: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
evidence.quote: It grows best in poor to average, well-drained soil in full sun, but with some afternoon shade in hot summers.
Heat stressed plants often produce leaves and flowers that may be more pungent than most people prefer.
If plants show signs of decline or become leggy during the summer, cut them back lightly and they will produce new growth for the remainder of the season.
They grow best in early summer and fall and should be kept watered during the hottest, driest part of the summer.

evidence.source_name: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
evidence.quote: Common nasturtium is a warm-weather annual with long stems, parasol-like leaves, and spurred 5-petaled flowers.
The distinctive nasturtium seedlings generally come up with 7-10 days of seeding and grow quickly in warm weather.
Sow seeds outdoors after the danger of frost has passed and the soil has had a chance to warm up.
Plant seeds from spring through fall throughout Florida and year-round in South Florida.

nasturtium.hold_basis: M only, qualitative: plants decline when temperatures get too hot (UF Charlotte, NCSU, Illinois). No G limit: T1 sources call it a warm-weather annual, say seedlings grow quickly in warm weather, and UF says sow spring through fall in Florida.
nasturtium.threshold_note: No T1 temperature found for either the bloom decline or a germination ceiling. A seed-gardening site (harvesttotable, not T1/T2-grade) claims bloom stops above 85°F; not used. A peer-reviewed SJST 2015 paper (Munir et al., 'Empress of India') reportedly found plant quality decreased at 25 and 30°C with best quality at 15-20°C, but the SJST and DOAJ pages could not be fetched (timeout / Cloudflare 403), so no verbatim quote; AGRIS record has no abstract text.
gaps: No T1 germination temperature or upper germination limit (extension pages give only 'after frost' / 'soil has had a chance to warm up' / 'depending on soil temperature').
No T1 numeric heat threshold for flowering decline.
Munir et al. 2015 SJST (temperature vs. quality) unfetchable: sjst.psu.ac.th timed out twice, doaj.org 403 to both user agents and WebFetch.
nasturtium.notes: T1 evidence is split. Mature-plant decline in heat is real (M), but the germination evidence points the other way (warm soil wanted, 'grow quickly in warm weather', UF sows spring through fall). A sowing hold rests only on 'new plants would grow into heat and decline', with no number, so Trevor must rule between (a) pause_in_heat true with a qualitative reason and the unsourced 85 fallback, or (b) pause_in_heat false. heat_effect 'heat_tolerant' is contradicted by the M quotes either way (UF Charlotte, NCSU); suggest a bloom/quality-loss value.

evidence.quote: If grown for culinary use, successive sowings of seed at four week intervals will result in a good supply of fresh foliage.

evidence.source_name: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
evidence.quote: Cut the plant back by a half in mid-summer for new growth for the fall.
Borage will bloom for many weeks if the older flowers are trimmed off, and you can often push tattered plants to make a comeback by pruning them back halfway in midsummer.
Plants fade in deep summer heat and humidity, but can be reseeded for late summer/early fall harvest.
Germination: 70°F, light required, 10 days.
Temperature and Humidity Borage is a particularly hardy herb and able to withstand high and low temperatures.
While it is tolerant of heat and cold weather, it is unable to withstand a hard frost.

borage.hold_basis: None at T1. Only a T2 seed catalog says plants fade in deep summer heat and humidity; a T2 master-gardener page says borage withstands high temperatures; Illinois Extension (T1) recommends 4-week successive sowings with no heat caveat.
borage.threshold_note: No temperature found at any tier for a borage heat limit or germination ceiling. A legacy Illinois State Water Survey alt-crops page (ECOCROP-style, reportedly 'Abs.Max=79°F, Opt.Max=72°F') is now a 404, so it is unverifiable.
gaps: No T1 source (NCSU, UC ANR x2, UF Nassau, Illinois, UMD, Wisconsin not present) states borage declines, stops flowering, or fails to germinate in heat.
borage.notes: The pause_in_heat=true value and the succession tip's 'borage declines and mildews in that heat' have no T1 support. RE-VERIFY of existing tip bor_germ_timing ('in hot, humid climates sow in fall... since borage struggles in extreme summer heat', sources ncsu_ext + uf_ifas): NCSU's page has no heat statement (only 'cut back by a half in mid-summer for new growth for the fall'), and the UF Nassau blog body says nothing about heat or timing (only its title question mentions November). Midsummer cut-back advice (NCSU, UC ANR) implies tired plants by midsummer but does not attribute it to heat. Recommend pause_in_heat false (coherent with heat_tolerant), or, if Trevor accepts T2, a qualitative hold citing Southern Exposure only.

The constant temperature of 10°C and 15°C, and alternated in 10°C/15°C and 10°C/20°C provided germination of the seeds superior to 80% in the end of 14th day.

chamomile.hold_basis: Only a general T1 'prefers cooler climates' (MSU). No T1 statement that chamomile declines, stops flowering, or fails to germinate in heat; Wisconsin says germination is fast under warm conditions.
chamomile.threshold_note: No usable temperature. Souza et al. tested only cool regimes (10-20°C) and shows good germination there, not an upper limit. The UFFS repository item says seeds did not germinate 'at high temperatures' among 24/32/40°C without saying which, and is student work (T2).
gaps: No T1 extension source on chamomile heat decline, flowering stop, or humidity/mildew (the existing weather_trigger 'declines in the heat and humidity ... powdery mildew or botrytis' cites msu_bozeman + uwi_hort; neither page contains heat, humidity, mildew or botrytis).
Nóbrega et al. (Revista Brasileira de Sementes, light and temperature on Matricaria recutita germination) page at abrates.org.br returned an empty body to both user agents.
chamomile.notes: pause_in_heat true is not supported at T1 beyond 'prefers cooler climates'. Trevor to rule: false (coherent with heat_tolerant) or keep a qualitative hold. Separately, the hot-humid weather_trigger and the succession tip's 'declines and molds' text appear unsourced by their cited pages (re-verified against cache bytes).
